extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity (researchers, academic administrators, science journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: News/blog post describing the outcome and surrounding issues in a specific academic-research-misconduct case (Diederik Stapel), including institutional and prosecutorial responses, whistleblower process, and commentary on sanctions and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIOD determination on misuse of public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: The FIOD (Dutch organisation that pursues tax, benefit and other frauds) states that Stapel has not misused public funds, because they were given for doing research that was performed. Most of it was spent on salaries and the personnel paid performed research. Although this was with made-up data, the implicated personnel did not know this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/prosecutorial standard used here: public funds are not considered 'misused' if they were disbursed for research work that was carried out (e.g., salaries paid) and if the paid personnel were unaware of data fabrication. This is the factual/legal rationale the prosecutor relied on in declining misuse charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific integrity violation / harm to doctoral students
rubrics_metrics.description: "Stapel has acted against scientific integrity and has harmed the interests of doctoral students that have worked with him," writes FIOD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional/prosecutorial finding that fabricating data constitutes a breach of scientific integrity and creates tangible harm to trainees; such findings can justify disciplinary or reputational consequences even if criminal misuse-of-funds charges are not sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions used in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stapel will do 120 hours of community service, and decline disability and illness benefits that would have added up to 18 months’ worth of salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of non-custodial sanctions and financial forfeiture applied in this case. Use as a reference for the kinds of penalties prosecutors or institutions may negotiate (community service, forfeiture/decline of benefits, revocation of degrees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntarily giving up PhD as mitigating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparently, it helped his case that he had voluntarily given up his PhD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/strategic point: surrendering a degree or otherwise accepting institutional sanction can be treated as a mitigating factor by prosecutors or negotiating parties when determining criminal or administrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower evidence-gathering and reporting process
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fraud was brought to light by three young researchers... They reported their suspicions of data falsification by Mr Stapel at the end of August 2011. After months of observation they had gathered sufficient details to demonstrate that something was amiss. The researchers all deserve praise for reporting these suspicions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes recommended whistleblower practice and institutional pathway: gather corroborating details over time before reporting, report to head of department, and expect the head to notify higher administration (Rector Magnificus) and engage with whistleblowers. Also notes whistleblowers' dependent position and the risks they face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to act on earlier reports (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Three young researchers had previously sounded the alarm... Two professors had previously observed data that were ‘too good to be true’. However, none of these earlier reports were acted upon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: institutions failing to act on prior warnings allows misconduct to persist. Effective institutional response requires timely investigation of earlier alerts and procedures that prevent ignoring or suppressing concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that fabricating data for grant applications is misuse/theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argue that 'He made up data in his grant applications that got funded. That is theft.' and ask 'If this (i.e. repeated and continuous fabrication of data that is entirely false, and is used for getting more public funds) is not misuse of public funds, then I do not know what the misuse of public funds is!?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewpoint/standard held by some stakeholders: knowingly fabricating data to secure grants should be treated as misuse of public funds (akin to theft) even if a prosecutor applies a narrower legal standard. This reflects a substantive normative criterion for evaluating severity of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for transparency and institutional accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Transparency Index which shows whether the editors/publishers/institutions Do_the_Right_Thing will make these parties MOTIVATED to Do_the_Right_Thing in all cases of reported misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed evaluative mechanism: public transparency metrics (indices) for journals/institutions to incentivize proper handling of misconduct. Use as a prescriptive criterion for institutional performance and trustworthiness.
